  \begin{revision}
  Do socio-emotional skills transmit socio-economic advantage in learning, and how does school composition change that pathway? Model-based multilevel mediation estimates using PISA 2025 cover 428,040 pupils in 67 systems. The joint pathway through 6 skills is positive at p < 0.05 in 52 systems and in 7 more systems at p < 0.10; 48 retain support at a 5\% false discovery rate. School sorting enlarges the pathway at p < 0.05 in 27 systems and in 9 more systems at p < 0.10, although a large between-school reading gradient need not have a large skills component. Recipient gains exceed gap reduction when advantaged classmates also gain through updated school skill means: in Korea, the respective projections are 28.21 and 20.74 points. The estimates describe socio-economic gradients in skills and their contribution to observed learning inequality; cross-sectional data do not identify the direction between skills and learning.

# Introduction

In 1976, Bowles and Gintis argued that schooling reproduces economic inequality partly through the non-cognitive traits it cultivates and rewards [@bowles1976; @bowles2002schooling]. Family advantage can be transmitted through dispositions, money, qualifications, and cognitive ability. Children encounter different conditions for developing the behaviors valued in school and, later, in employment. Their correspondence argument placed the organization of schooling and work at the center of this process. The question behind today's interest in socio-emotional skills is therefore not new. It is whether characteristics that appear personal help convert unequal family circumstances into unequal educational outcomes.

Modern economics of skill formation gives this question a production interpretation. Families invest time and resources. Schools supply instruction and learning environments, and existing capabilities affect what children gain from subsequent investment [@cunha2007]. Curiosity can encourage exploration, while perseverance can sustain effort. Advantaged families may have more opportunities to cultivate these dispositions and secure access to settings in which they support learning. This account differs from explaining rewards through conformity to workplace hierarchies, but it shares the concern that non-cognitive characteristics help transmit economic advantage. The present study examines the learning pathway, with school composition retained as part of the comparison.

```{=latex}
\begin{revision}
```

This paper examines the socio-economic gradient in socio-emotional skills and how their relationship with learning helps describe the reproduction of educational advantage. Socio-economic inequality in achievement is well established; comparative evidence on specific socio-emotional skills and their place within school inequality is less extensive. Existing cross-country studies already document unequal skill distributions [@gruijters2024; @avanesian2025]. The contribution of this study is that it connects those distributions to learning inequality across 67 systems, distinguishes within-school patterns from school composition, and assesses the distributional importance of skill differences under a common fitted learning response.

```{=latex}
\end{revision}
```

Previous research also establishes that socio-emotional characteristics contribute to socio-economic achievement gaps. @hofer2024 estimate joint and separate self-perception mediation in reading, while @gruijters2024 distinguish skill endowments from their achievement returns in a counterfactual decomposition of the science gap. The unresolved issue addressed in this study is how school composition changes the interpretation of that contribution. A large reading gap between school intakes can coexist with a small measured skills pathway. Predicted gains for disadvantaged pupils can also exceed the reduction in their disadvantage. I connect these questions by locating the skills pathway within the wider school gradient and accounting for predicted changes among both recipients and their advantaged classmates under skill equalization. Within each country, I hold the fitted reading response common across socio-economic status (SES) groups and examine school composition. This differs from decomposing group-specific returns to skills.

```{=latex}
\begin{revision}
```

I use the student and school data from PISA 2025 and estimate each education system separately. The main comparison covers 67 systems that provide reading scores as a measure of learning and have data available on all 6 socio-emotional skills: perseverance, curiosity, enjoyment of problem solving, cognitive adaptability, goal setting, and self-regulated help seeking. Together they contribute 428,040 pupils in 18,836 schools.

```{=latex}
\end{revision}
```

The joint skills pathway is positive at p < 0.05 in 52 of the 67 systems, with 7 more systems at p < 0.10; 48 retain support at a 5% false discovery rate after correction for multiple testing. The 3 largest point estimates are Korea (`r fmt(est('KOR','skills_sorting'))` reading points per 10 national SES rank points), Japan (`r fmt(est('JPN','skills_sorting'))`), and Ecuador (`r fmt(est('ECU','skills_sorting'))`). Curiosity is the most widespread individual contributor, but Korea's strongest positive contributions include enjoyment of problem solving and goal setting.

In a counterfactual manner, I also ask a distributional question: how much would the reading gap change if pupils in the lower national SES quartile received the joint skill distribution of the upper quartile, while their socio-economic circumstances and school membership stayed fixed? I update school-average skills along with individual skills. The projected gap narrows at p < 0.05 in 57 systems, with 5 more systems at p < 0.10; 56 retain support at a 5% false discovery rate after a separate adjustment across these country comparisons. In Korea, the recipient group's predicted gain is `r fmt(cfest('KOR','recipient_change'))` points, but the upper-quartile group also gains `r fmt(cfest('KOR','reference_change'))` points through the change in school skill composition. The gap consequently narrows by `r fmt(cfest('KOR','gap_reduction'))` points. This distinguishes the size of a recipient gain from its equalizing effect.


The between-school contribution exceeds the within-school contribution to the total gradient, with a difference at p < 0.05 in 46 systems and in 1 more system at p < 0.10. For the skills pathway, the corresponding counts are 14 and 8. These counts compare contributions at 2 levels; they do not measure the fraction of inequality explained by skills. Germany illustrates the substantive distinction: a large between-school gradient coexists with a small, uncertain skills-mediated component. Skills can transmit advantage while accounting for only part of school-level inequality.

The development-policy question is how support directed at pupils' skills should relate to investment in the schools they attend. This distinguishes 2 margins for allocating scarce educational resources: helping disadvantaged pupils acquire and use skills, and improving the environments in which those pupils learn. The estimates diagnose how much of the observed inequality a skills account can explain and whether projected benefits extend beyond recipients. Comparing programs still requires evidence on achievable skill changes, causal learning responses, and costs. Country-specific estimates show how the relevance of skills policies varies across systems.

# Previous evidence and research questions

## Skill formation and the transmission of advantage

The economics of skill formation treats skills as products of cumulative investment and as inputs into subsequent learning. Family resources influence the time, materials, and experiences available to children; existing capabilities influence what children gain from later investment [@cunha2007]. Socio-emotional skills can enter this process through attention, persistence, and engagement with difficult tasks. A pupil's capacity to organize study may therefore reflect past opportunities while also affecting the use of current educational inputs.

Economic research emphasizes that these capabilities are multidimensional and that their measurement depends on behavior and context [@almlund2011]. In this study, socio-emotional skills refer to 6 questionnaire scales administered in PISA 2025: perseverance, curiosity, enjoyment of problem solving, cognitive adaptability, goal setting, and self-regulated help seeking. Cognitive adaptability is a self-report measure of how pupils adapt their approach. Keeping the scales separate allows family advantage to have different relationships with each disposition.

The OECD's SSES framework organizes socio-emotional skills as facets of the Big Five personality domains [@kankaras2019]. The 6 PISA indices cover task-performance and open-mindedness facets alongside related learning strategies. They provide partial coverage of the Big Five domains.


Evidence from a randomized intervention in Colombia connects parental investments to improvements in early development [@attanasio2020]. At school age, teachers affect outcomes beyond test scores that predict later educational attainment [@jackson2018]. These findings give families and schools a role in producing capabilities, although neither establishes the size of adolescent skill inequalities in the present sample. In cross-country evidence, @gruijters2024 find socio-economic differences in the socio-emotional characteristics measured in PISA 2018. Their contribution to achievement inequality varies substantially.

```{=latex}
\begin{revision}
```

The investment account predicts that family advantage accompanies opportunities to develop skills that support learning [@cunha2007]. Parental education generally precedes adolescents' measured skills, making reverse causality less immediate than in the skills--achievement relationship. This temporal ordering does not make socio-economic status exogenous: household resources and parental employment can respond to children's needs, while shared family characteristics can influence both background and skills. The estimated gradients establish stratification, rather than the causal productivity of parental investment.

```{=latex}
\end{revision}
```

> *RQ1a. How is socio-economic rank related to each socio-emotional skill within and between schools?*

```{=latex}
\begin{revision}
```

A socially stratified skill contributes statistically to the achievement gradient when it also predicts achievement after the other measured skills enter. @hofer2024 examine joint and separate self-perception mediation across 70 PISA 2018 countries, while @gruijters2024 find a modest skills contribution to socio-economic science gaps. In the present analysis, the direction from skills to reading follows an economic production interpretation. Cross-sectional observations also permit learning to influence skills, and common causes to influence both. The resulting mediation contrasts quantify a theory-guided accounting relationship; they do not identify a one-way transmission mechanism.

```{=latex}
\end{revision}
```

> *RQ1b. How much socio-economic advantage in reading is transmitted jointly through the 6 skills?*

The economic distinction is between capabilities that sustain investment in learning and those that influence how learning opportunities are used. Task-performance dispositions, including perseverance, can help pupils maintain effort when immediate rewards are small or tasks are difficult. Open-mindedness, including curiosity, can encourage information seeking and engagement with unfamiliar ideas. Different dispositions may affect time spent studying and the learning gained from that time [@cunha2007; @almlund2011]. The joint model therefore retains a separate contribution for each skill.

A skill's contribution also requires a socio-economic gradient in its distribution. An evenly distributed skill contributes little to the gradient even if it strongly predicts reading. A strongly stratified skill also contributes little when its reading relationship is weak after other skills enter. Earlier decomposition work distinguishes such differences in endowments from differences in returns [@gruijters2024]. I therefore compare the joint-model contributions across skills and systems without imposing a universal ranking or assuming every contribution is positive.

> *RQ1c. Which skills contribute to this transmission?*

## School allocation and the location of the gradient

Families transmit access to educational environments alongside individual capabilities [@bowles2002inheritance]. School resources and the organization of instruction can affect learning through several inputs. @leon2015 document unequal school resources and achievement in Peru. Cross-country evidence from @hanushek2006 suggests that early tracking increases achievement inequality. These studies establish school allocation as a potential channel of socio-economic inequality.

@asadullah2021 examine effort, preferences, and family circumstances in rural Bangladesh, allocating predicted achievement variance within and between schools. Their analysis shows why individual learning inputs and school-level inequality should be considered together. The present question concerns a different object: the reading gradient accompanying a change in national SES rank and the gap projected under skill equalization. Separating these objects matters because the location of overall achievement variation does not establish how much of a socio-economic gradient is carried by particular skills. Socio-emotional measures are treated here as potentially unequal learning inputs, without attributing responsibility for those inequalities to pupils.

School production involves several inputs, and schools' contributions to achievement and socio-emotional development need not coincide. Using value-added models for Chicago high schools, @jackson2020school find that schools' contributions to social well-being and hard work predict later attainment beyond their contributions to test scores. Instruction also responds to pupil composition. In a randomized tracking experiment in Kenya, @duflo2011tracking find that lower-achieving pupils benefit when teachers adapt instruction to their level, despite separation from higher-achieving peers. Together, these findings motivate examining measured skills alongside the other inputs through which schools support learning. A large between-school reading gradient may therefore contain a substantial component outside the measured skills pathway. What remains unclear is how much of the inequality between school intakes is carried by socio-emotional skills, compared with the skills pathway among pupils attending the same school.

> *RQ2a. How are the total reading gradient and its skills-mediated component distributed within and between schools?*

School sorting concerns how these learning inputs are distributed across pupils. In Romania, @popeleches2013 find that access to higher-achieving secondary schools improves graduation-test performance, while their evidence also reveals teacher sorting and reduced parental effort when children enter better schools. School allocation thus brings together differences in pupil characteristics, teaching, and family responses. For socio-emotional skills, the implication is that family advantage may be transmitted through both a pupil's own capabilities and access to school environments with different skill profiles. Existing evidence on school effectiveness and tracking does not establish the size of this particular pathway. It leaves 2 related questions: where the skills contribution to the reading gradient is concentrated, and whether the school composition accompanying family advantage amplifies that contribution.

> *RQ2b. How much does observed school sorting add to the skills pathway?*

## Skill endowments and the achievement gap

@avanesian2025 provide relevant evidence using OECD SSES data on 44,394 pupils aged 10 and 15 in 8 cities. Their mixed-effects models relate 5 broad skill domains to a grade-based high-achievement indicator. Task performance and open-mindedness are the strongest positive predictors; the relationships for other domains are less uniform, including a nonlinear collaboration pattern. Their comparison of SES groups also shows why similar skill levels need not eliminate an achievement gap: the high-SES advantage persists, and the plotted task-performance and open-mindedness slopes are largely parallel. These results motivate distinguishing the contribution of particular skills from a general claim that more non-cognitive skill necessarily equalizes achievement.

@gruijters2024 distinguish differences in skill endowments from differences in their achievement returns. Their counterfactual decomposition attributes a modest part of the socio-economic science gap to the measured skills, predominantly through endowment differences. A skill can therefore contribute to achievement while equalizing that skill leaves much of the gap intact. In the production framework of @cunha2007, equalizing 1 input leaves other inputs and earlier investments unequal.

> *RQ3a. How would disadvantaged pupils' reading change if their skill profiles matched those of advantaged pupils?*

The distributional case for skills development therefore depends on how improvements translate into learning under unequal educational conditions. Complementarity between capabilities and subsequent investment implies that similar skill gains need not produce similar achievement gains across learning environments [@cunha2007]. Evidence that peer composition and the organization of instruction jointly affect learning adds a further consideration: benefits may extend beyond the pupils whose capabilities improve [@duflo2011tracking]. Whether those benefits mainly reach disadvantaged pupils or are shared with more advantaged classmates matters for the achievement gap. The unresolved question is how much reducing skill inequalities could narrow that gap when learning takes place in socially differentiated schools.

> *RQ3b. How much would the socio-economic reading gap narrow after accounting for predicted changes among advantaged classmates?*

# Data and empirical strategy

## Sample, outcome, and socio-economic rank

*Sample.* I use the PISA 2025 student and school files [@oecd2026data], retaining 67 systems with all 6 skill indices. Models require valid reading scores, ESCS, age, gender, school identifiers, and survey weights, with at least 100 complete pupils and 30 schools. The analytic sample contains 428,040 pupils in 18,836 schools. All skill and achievement equations use the same pupils within each system. Complete-case coverage is lowest in Armenia (21.6%) and Lebanon (30.1%); retained pupils score approximately 40 and 52 reading points higher than excluded pupils with observed reading. Appendix Table A2 reports country coverage; Tables A5–A6 document complete-case selection in Armenia and Lebanon.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-descriptives
#| results: asis
ids<-A[exposure=='SES'][order(economy),CNT]
z<-rbindlist(lapply(ids,function(cc){
 ms<-function(v,ex='SES'){a<-DS[CNT==cc&exposure==ex&variable==v];if(!nrow(a))return('—');paste0(fmt(a$mean,if(v=='ESCS')2 else 1),' (',fmt(a$SD,if(v=='ESCS')2 else 1),')')}
 data.table(System=G[CNT==cc,economy],Pupils=num(A[CNT==cc&exposure=='SES',N]),Schools=num(A[CNT==cc&exposure=='SES',schools]),Reading=ms('Reading'),ESCS=ms('ESCS'))
}))
tbl(z,'Country descriptive statistics for the socio-economic-rank analysis. Reading and ESCS: weighted mean (SD). Pupil and school counts are unweighted. Reading descriptives use each pupil’s average of 10 plausible values.',size=8,widths=c('3.8cm','1.8cm','1.8cm','3cm','2.7cm'))
```

*Outcome: reading achievement.* The outcome is the PISA reading score, represented by 10 plausible values that are analyzed separately and then combined. In the socio-economic-rank analytic samples, student-weighted country means range from `r fmt(DS[CNT=='MAR' & exposure=='SES' & variable=='Reading',mean],1)` points in Morocco to `r fmt(DS[CNT=='SGP' & exposure=='SES' & variable=='Reading',mean],1)` in Singapore. Within-country standard deviations range from `r fmt(min(DS[exposure=='SES' & variable=='Reading',SD]),1)` to `r fmt(max(DS[exposure=='SES' & variable=='Reading',SD]),1)` points. Descriptive means and standard deviations are calculated from each pupil's average across the 10 reading plausible values. @tbl-descriptives reports the weighted reading mean and SD for every system. All models retain the original reading-point scale. Appendix Table A7 reports country means and standard deviations for reading, SES rank, and ESCS.

*Exposure: socio-economic rank.* Family status is measured by PISA's index of economic, social, and cultural status (ESCS). I convert ESCS to a weighted midpoint percentile rank within each system, using all pupils with valid ESCS and final student weights before complete-case selection. Dividing by 10 makes 1 unit a 10-percentile-point difference in national socio-economic position, rather than an income percentage or a common absolute resource difference across countries.

*Mediators: 6 socio-emotional skills.* The OECD's Survey on Social and Emotional Skills (SSES) organizes skills as facets of a Big Five-based taxonomy [@kankaras2019]. Perseverance and goal setting concern conscientiousness (task performance); curiosity and enjoyment of problem solving concern openness (open-mindedness). Cognitive adaptability overlaps openness and emotional stability, while help seeking combines self-regulation with cooperation, conceptually related to conscientiousness and agreeableness. For the latter 4 PISA scales these are content-based correspondences, not validated 1-to-1 Big Five subscales; the 6 indices do not measure a full Big Five inventory. I use the released weighted-likelihood indices, standardized to mean 0 and SD 1 in each country's weighted analytic sample. All 6 enter jointly, with no imputation of missing indices. Appendix Table A4 maps the indices to questionnaire items [@oecd2025questionnaire; @oecd2025codebook].

## Econometric strategy

### Models and research questions

For each country, I estimate random-intercept models with pupils nested in schools. Every exposure, skill, and control enters as a within-school deviation ($Z^W_{ij}=Z_{ij}-\bar Z_j$) and a weighted school mean ($\bar Z_j$). This correlated-effects specification [@mundlak1978] separates comparisons among classmates from comparisons between school intakes. It retains the observed composition associated with non-random school allocation instead of absorbing all between-school variation into fixed effects.

*Exposure-to-skill gradients.* I fit a separate equation for each skill $k$, with $X$ denoting socio-economic rank divided by 10:

$$
M_{kij}=\alpha_k+a_{Wk}X^W_{ij}+a_{Bk}\bar X_j+
\gamma_{Wk}'C^W_{ij}+\gamma_{Bk}'\bar C_j+u_{kj}+e_{kij}.
$$ {#eq-m1}

The $a_W$ and $a_B$ coefficients measure the exposure-to-skill gradients within and between schools. Controls $C$ comprise age and the recorded non-male gender indicator, entered at both levels. All equations use the same pupils and school means within each system.

*Joint skills pathway.* The achievement equation includes all 6 skills jointly:

$$
\begin{split}
Y_{ij}={}&\alpha+c'_WX^W_{ij}+c'_B\bar X_j+
\sum_{k=1}^{6}\{b_{Wk}M^W_{kij}+b_{Bk}\bar M_{kj}\}\\
&+\beta_W'C^W_{ij}+\beta_B'\bar C_j+v_j+\epsilon_{ij}.
\end{split}
$$ {#eq-m2}

The reading coefficients measure how each skill relates to achievement among classmates and between school intakes, holding the other skills and controls constant. I refer to the skill equations as M1 and the joint reading equation as M2. A baseline model, M0, omits the skills.

*Joint pathway and individual contributions.* For each skill, I multiply its socio-economic gradient by its reading coefficient at the corresponding school level. Adding the 6 products gives the joint skills pathway. This calculation compares predicted reading under the skill profiles associated with a 10-point difference in socio-economic rank, holding the reading equation's exposure and controls fixed. Under the additive model, these products equal the model-based mediation contrast obtained by integrating over the joint skill distribution [@imai2010; @preacher2010; @vansteelandt2017]. The skills need not have independent residuals.

I report both a contrast entirely among classmates and a contrast that incorporates the school composition accompanying family rank. The latter uses a student-weighted regression of school-average rank on individual rank and controls. Each skill's contribution is its part of the joint pathway. The reported skills share divides this pathway by the model-implied total gradient, which also includes the remaining exposure relationship. Shares are withheld when denominators are unstable or components have opposing signs.

*Concentration of the gradient.* The within--between decomposition divides the same total gradient into contributions from differences among classmates and differences between school intakes. I then separate each contribution into the part associated with the measured skills and the remainder. Differences between the 2 school-level contributions are calculated within each bootstrap and plausible-value draw.

*School sorting.* The sorting increment is the difference between the pathway incorporating observed school composition and the pathway for a 10-point rank difference entirely among classmates. It measures how much the observed allocation of pupils across schools adds to the skills pathway. This comparison can be positive even when the within-school contribution is larger than the between-school contribution. Appendix Section II gives the exact identities and country estimates.

*Recipient gains and gap reduction.* The equalization exercise replaces the joint skill profiles of pupils in the bottom national SES quartile with the student-weighted distribution among top-quartile pupils. The replacement preserves the skills' observed combinations. Socio-economic rank, controls, and school membership remain fixed. School-average skills change consistently with the recipients' new profiles.

The fitted reading model predicts changes for recipients and for classmates whose own profiles remain unchanged. Subtracting the comparison group's average gain from recipients' average gain gives the reduction in the reading gap. This exercise uses the observed differences between the 2 groups' skill distributions. The mediation calculation instead uses skill differences associated with a specified increment in socio-economic rank. Appendix Section III gives the prediction formula and country estimates.

### Statistical implementation

```{=latex}
\begin{revision}
```

The manuscript adheres to the principles of literate programming [@knuth1984]. Quarto [@quarto] integrates the text with R 4.4.1 [@rcore2024], drawing statistical results directly from the reproducible code. Survey-weighted random-intercept models use a custom R implementation checked against WeMix 4.0.3 [@wemix]; unweighted sensitivity models use `lme4` [@bates2015]. Custom R routines calculate mediation, individual skill contributions, within--between decomposition, and equalization from the fitted models. Confidence intervals incorporate 499 school-bootstrap resamples and 10 reading plausible values. To account for testing many hypotheses, Benjamini--Hochberg adjustments target a 5% false discovery rate---the expected proportion of false positives among rejected hypotheses---within each test family [@benjamini1995]. These adjustments use R's bundled `stats` package. Charts report unadjusted significance and equal-weight system means; adjusted support is identified separately. Appendix Table A1 summarizes uncertainty estimation and test-family definitions.

```{=latex}
\end{revision}
```

## The combined skills pathway carries advantage in most systems

@fig-ses displays all 67 country estimates, with and without the school component; Appendix Table A11 reports the estimates and sorting increments; Table A13 reports the total gradient, remaining component, and admissible skills share. The pathway allowing for sorting is positive at p < 0.05 in 52 systems and in 7 more systems at p < 0.10; the remaining 8 do not reach p < 0.10. No negative pathway reaches p < 0.10. After adjustment for multiple testing, 48 retain support at a 5% false discovery rate. The result is broad evidence for a skills route, alongside meaningful variation in its magnitude and precision.

The equal-weight mean joint pathway is `r mean_ci('skills_sorting')` reading points per 10 SES rank points. The worked examples show how its size differs across systems. Denmark's pathway is `r ci('DNK','skills_sorting')` reading points per 10 SES rank points, accounting for `r fmt(est('DNK','share'),1)`% of its model-implied total gradient. Malaysia's pathway is `r ci('MYS','skills_sorting')` points and `r fmt(est('MYS','share'),1)`%. Korea's is `r ci('KOR','skills_sorting')` points and `r fmt(est('KOR','share'),1)`%. For Malaysia, the `r fmt(est('MYS','skills_sorting'))`-point contrast means that predicted reading at the higher socio-economic profile falls by that amount when its joint skill profile is replaced by the one accompanying a profile 10 SES rank points lower, with the other inputs held fixed. These percentages concern different national gradients. They do not imply that Korea has the largest overall SES gap or that its schools generate the largest causal return to a skills program.

Germany and Mongolia provide a useful counterpoint: their pathways are not statistically significant. A small or uncertain net pathway can arise from weak links or from offsetting skill contributions; it does not require every skill to be unrelated to achievement. These estimates are retained alongside the positive cases.

Systems appear alphabetically, and both panels use the same horizontal scale.}](../04_output/rev2/figures/ses_pathways.pdf){#fig-ses width=100% fig-pos='H'}

\clearpage

## Which skills carry the pathway?

Curiosity is the most widespread positive contributor: its individual pathway is positive in `r count_bands('indS_CURIO')`. The corresponding counts are `r count_bands('indS_PERSEV')` for perseverance, `r count_bands('indS_COGABIL')` for cognitive adaptability, `r count_bands('indS_ENPROBS')` for enjoyment of problem solving, `r count_bands('indS_SELFREG')` for self-regulated help seeking, and `r count_bands('indS_GOALSET')` for goal setting. These counts concern contributions after all 6 skills enter together, rather than separate regressions giving each skill credit for shared variation.

@fig-ses-skills shows the complete country pattern; Appendix Table A19 reports each contribution and its standard error. Curiosity contributes `r ci('DNK','indS_CURIO')` reading points in Denmark and `r ci('MYS','indS_CURIO')` in Malaysia. Korea is different. Its curiosity contribution is `r ci('KOR','indS_CURIO')`, while enjoyment of problem solving contributes `r ci('KOR','indS_ENPROBS')` and goal setting `r ci('KOR','indS_GOALSET')`. The combined Korean pathway is strong even though curiosity does not carry it clearly.

Goal setting, measured through planning study, checking understanding, and adapting strategies, illustrates another distinction. Its within-school social gradient is positive in `r count_bands('aW_GOALSET')`, yet its joint contribution to reading is positive in `r count_bands('indS_GOALSET')` and negative in `r count_bands('indS_GOALSET',negative=TRUE)`. The remaining systems do not reach p < 0.10. The data therefore do not support treating a socially advantaged disposition as automatically productive for reading, conditional on the other skills. The pattern is compatible with differences in what the scale measures in practice, overlaps among dispositions, and the uses to which pupils put them. It does not imply that setting goals generally damages learning.

![Skill-specific contributions to the socio-economic pathway in every full-6-skill system. \figurenote{Colors show reading points, with zero at the center. White circles denote p < 0.05 and triangles p < 0.10; unmarked cells are not significant (unadjusted, 2-sided). Symbols indicate the strongest threshold met; not significant refers to the 10\% level. The single mean row averages country-specific contributions with equal weights. Persev. denotes perseverance; Adapt., cognitive adaptability; Problem solving, enjoyment of problem solving; and Help seeking, self-regulated help seeking. Each country cell is part of the same joint model; cells sum across skills to the country pathway in Figure~\ref{fig-ses}.}](../04_output/rev2/figures/ses_skills.pdf){#fig-ses-skills width=100% fig-pos='H'}

\clearpage

## Within- and between-school contributions to the reading gradient

@fig-within-between decomposes each country's total gradient into within- and between-school contributions. Each bar separates the skills-mediated part from the remainder. The between-school contribution is larger in `r count_bands('total_between_minus_within',kind='decomposition')`; `r wbcount('total_between_minus_within',TRUE)` retain support at a 5% false discovery rate after adjustment. For the skills-mediated part, the counts are `r count_bands('skills_between_minus_within',kind='decomposition')`, with `r wbcount('skills_between_minus_within',TRUE)` retaining adjusted support at the same threshold. Germany illustrates the distinction. Its between-school contribution is `r wbci('DEU','total_between')` reading points, of which `r wbci('DEU','skills_between')` points run through the measured skills. Most of its between-school gradient is therefore in the remaining component.

In Korea, the total gradient comprises `r wbci('KOR','total_within')` points within schools and `r wbci('KOR','total_between')` between schools. Skills account for `r wbci('KOR','skills_within')` and `r wbci('KOR','skills_between')` points, respectively. The estimated skills contribution is larger between schools, but the difference is not statistically significant. This comparison differs from the positive sorting increment reported below. The allocation divides the combined profile contrast into 2 parts; the sorting increment compares that combined contrast with a 10-point difference entirely among classmates. Appendix Tables A15–A16 report country-specific components, and Table A17 reports the difference tests.

\clearpage

![Within- and between-school contributions to the socio-economic reading gradient in all 67 systems. \figurenote{The final row gives equal-weight means across systems. For each country, the upper bar shows the within-school contribution and the lower bar shows the between-school contribution. Dark segments show the skills-mediated part. Black capped lines give 95\% intervals for each level's net contribution, calculated from paired school-bootstrap draws and 10 plausible values. Negative segments are retained to the left of zero. Appendix Tables A16–A17 report component-specific standard errors and direct between-minus-within tests.}](../04_output/rev2/figures/ses_within_between_composition.pdf){#fig-within-between width=100% fig-pos='H'}

\clearpage

## School sorting changes how much advantage runs through skills

The sorting comparison asks whether the skills pathway is larger when it incorporates the school composition accompanying family rank. It differs from asking where the total gradient and its skills component are concentrated. The additional pathway is positive at p < 0.05 in 27 of the 67 systems and in 9 more systems at p < 0.10, with 23 retaining support at a 5% false discovery rate after adjustment. @fig-sorting-addition shows the country estimates. Its equal-weight mean is `r mean_ci('sorting_increment')` reading points. In the remaining 31 systems, the addition is not statistically significant. No negative addition is statistically significant.

Korea's pathway rises from `r ci('KOR','skills_same_school')` points with school setting fixed to `r ci('KOR','skills_sorting')` when sorting is included. The addition itself is `r ci('KOR','sorting_increment')` points. Malaysia's corresponding addition is `r ci('MYS','sorting_increment')`. The differences between the 2 estimates are calculated in each bootstrap draw to obtain their confidence intervals.

Denmark shows why sorting should be estimated rather than assumed to amplify the route. Its fixed-setting pathway is `r ci('DNK','skills_same_school')` and its sorting addition is `r ci('DNK','sorting_increment')`. The joint pathway is positive, but the school extension adds little. Differences among classmates account for most of the estimated skill route in that comparison.

The economic implication is that a student-level account can miss an appreciable part of skill-mediated inequality in some systems. It does not follow that all school socio-economic differences operate through the measured skills. The remaining component continues to contain other connections between resources, schools, and reading. Nor is a positive sorting addition the effect of moving a pupil to a different school: it is the contribution of the observed school component to the specified profile contrast.

\clearpage

![Additional skills pathway associated with school sorting. \figurenote{Each point is the additional skills pathway associated with sorting, in reading points per 10 national socio-economic rank points. Bars are 95\% intervals calculated for the difference within the school-bootstrap and plausible-value procedure. Positive values indicate a larger pathway when observed school composition is included. Shapes distinguish unadjusted p-value bands; color identifies support after BH adjustment across the joint-pathway and sorting-addition family. All 67 systems remain visible. The final row is the equal-weight mean, shown as a black diamond with an unadjusted interval.}](../04_output/rev2/figures/ses_sorting_increment.pdf){#fig-sorting-addition width=100% fig-pos='H'}

\clearpage

## Equalizing skill profiles: recipient gains, and gap reduction

The full-profile replacement narrows the SES reading gap at p < 0.05 in 57 of 67 systems and in 5 more systems at p < 0.10; 56 retain support at a 5% false discovery rate after multiple-testing adjustment. The remaining 5 do not reach p < 0.10. @fig-equalization retains all systems. These results concern a specified change in skill endowments and school skill means, rather than a 10-SES-rank-point exposure contrast.

The equal-weight mean projected gap reduction is `r mean_ci('gap_reduction',kind='equalisation')` reading points. The difference between recipient gains, and gap reduction matters economically. In Korea, the observed upper--lower-quartile reading gap is `r fmt(cfest('KOR','baseline_gap'))` points. Recipients gain `r cfci('KOR','recipient_change')` points under replacement, while the upper-quartile group gains `r cfci('KOR','reference_change')`. The gap reduction is therefore `r cfci('KOR','gap_reduction')` points, or `r fmt(cfest('KOR','gap_fraction'),1)`% of the observed gap. Counting only recipients' gains would overstate the reduction in inequality. The reference-group change arises from the fitted school-composition response, with school membership fixed. @fig-recipient-gap compares these quantities for Korea and for the equal-weight mean across systems. Appendix Tables A25–A26 report the country estimates, and Table A29 describes the recipient and reference groups.


![Recipient gains and gap reduction under skill equalization in Korea and across the 67 systems. \figurenote{Recipients are pupils in the lower national socio-economic quartile; the comparison group is the upper quartile. The net gap reduction equals the recipient gain minus the comparison-group gain. Bars show recipient gains, the subtraction of comparison-group gains, and the resulting gap reduction. The 95\% intervals are shown for recipient gains and gap reduction; the middle subtraction has no interval. Country intervals use saved joint school-bootstrap and plausible-value calculations. Mean intervals combine independent country variances with equal weights. School membership stays fixed and school-average skills update with the recipient profiles.}](../04_output/rev2/figures/ses_recipient_gap_korea.pdf){#fig-recipient-gap width=100% fig-pos='H'}

In Denmark, the corresponding reduction is `r cfci('DNK','gap_reduction')` points, or `r fmt(cfest('DNK','gap_fraction'),1)`% of the gap. Malaysia's is `r cfci('MYS','gap_reduction')` points, or `r fmt(cfest('MYS','gap_fraction'),1)`%. Germany's reduction accounts for `r cfci('DEU','gap_reduction')` points. Mongolia, whose original joint SES pathway is uncertain, has a positive equalization contrast of `r cfci('MNG','gap_reduction')` points. The 2 exercises use different skill differences: fitted exposure gradients in the mediation calculation, and observed recipient--donor distributions in the replacement. Their significance counts should not be treated as replications of the same test.

\clearpage

![Projected reductions in the upper--lower-quartile reading gap after joint skill-profile replacement. \figurenote{All 67 6-skill systems and their equal-weight mean are shown. School membership, socio-economic rank, and controls stay fixed; school skill means change consistently with recipients' profiles. Shapes mark unadjusted 2-sided p-value bands shown in the legend. Bars combine the original school-bootstrap coefficient draws with resampled donor profiles, group weights, and reading plausible values.}](../04_output/rev2/figures/ses_equalization.pdf){#fig-equalization width=100% fig-pos='H'}

\clearpage

## Robustness checks

Alternative weighting and school-size restrictions preserve every country-specific counterfactual point estimate's direction. Across the main specification and all 3 checks, positive estimates are supported in `r retained_band(.05)` systems at p < 0.05 and `r retained_band(.10)-retained_band(.05)` more systems at p < 0.10. These use unscaled conditional student weights, schools with at least 10 analytic pupils, and unweighted random-intercept estimation. Each check refits M2 within 499 school resamples and recomputes donor profiles and group gaps. Appendix Figure A6 compares the alternative specifications, and Tables A34–A36 report their country-specific estimates and standard errors.

# Discussion

## \colorbox{cyan!8!white}{Socio-economic gradient of skills and educational advantage}

```{=latex}
\begin{revision}
```

The findings document a socio-economic gradient in socio-emotional skills and a positive joint model-based pathway at p < 0.05 in 52 of 67 systems, with 7 more systems at p < 0.10. This pattern is consistent with Bowles and Gintis's account of socially differentiated dispositions and with an investment account of unequal skill formation [@bowles1976; @cunha2007]. Curiosity contributes most widely, while Korea's profile gives greater importance to enjoyment of problem solving and goal setting.

```{=latex}
\end{revision}
```

@bowles1976 placed non-cognitive traits within the reproduction of economic inequality. Bowles, Gintis, and Osborne subsequently distinguished productive capabilities from preferences that help employers elicit effort [@bowles2001behavioral; @bowles2001incentive]. The reading outcome in this study concerns demonstrated proficiency before labor-market entry. Its interpretation is closer to the skill-formation framework of @cunha2007, in which earlier capabilities and investments influence the productivity of later investment. The measured social gradients and reading relationships support examining unequal skill formation as a possible source of learning inequality.

```{=latex}
\begin{revision}
```

Skills can be both products of educational experience and inputs into subsequent learning. Curiosity may encourage exploration, while successful learning may stimulate further curiosity. Such feedback is compatible with self-productivity and complementarity in skill formation [@cunha2007], but is not identified by the present cross-section. Differences across grades are reported in [Appendix Figure A7](ijed_ses_seg_supplement_rev2.pdf#nameddest=appendix-grade). Measured skill profiles differ across grades. Those comparisons involve different pupils, so selection, schooling, and self-reporting may each contribute to the pattern. The direction of change within individual pupils remains unresolved. Pupils who struggle with learning may intensify planning and corrective study strategies [@almlund2011]. That response could contribute to goal setting's negative conditional reading relationship.

```{=latex}
\end{revision}
```

## School allocation extends the skills pathway without exhausting school inequality

The within--between decomposition locates the socio-economic reading gradient and identifies the skills contribution at each level. Germany's large between-school contribution is mostly outside the measured skills pathway. Korea allocates a substantial part of its between-school point estimate to skills. The 46 systems with a larger between-school total contribution and the 14 with a larger between-school skills contribution describe separate comparisons. Those counts cannot establish the share of school inequality attributable to skills.

Sorting changes the exposure comparison. It asks how the combined skills pathway differs from a full 10-SES-rank-point contrast entirely among classmates. Its positive increment in Korea can coexist with an uncertain difference between the allocated within- and between-school skills contributions. Decomposition locates the gradient across school levels. The sorting comparison shows how much of the skills pathway accompanies the school composition associated with family rank.

Families transmit access to learning environments alongside individual characteristics [@bowles2002inheritance]. Evidence that early tracking increases achievement inequality [@hanushek2006] and that school-finance reforms improve disadvantaged children's later outcomes [@jackson2016spending] gives economic reasons to examine school institutions and resources. These studies do not identify the remaining component in the present decomposition. That component can include prior achievement, unmeasured capabilities, and differences in educational inputs. Teachers can also affect non-test-score outcomes predictive of attainment [@jackson2018], so school composition may reflect skill formation as well as opportunities to use existing skills. Longitudinal evidence is needed to distinguish those processes.

## Skill endowments and the scope for reducing inequality

The positive projected gap reduction at p < 0.05 in 57 systems, with 5 more systems at p < 0.10, places unequal skill endowments among the sources of socio-economic achievement inequality. This finding accords with @gruijters2024, who distinguish differences in skill endowments from differences in their achievement returns. Their PISA 2018 analysis attributes a modest part of the science gap to measured skills, mainly through endowment differences. The present results extend that question to reading and school skill composition: the distributional contribution of skills includes predicted changes among pupils whose own profiles remain unchanged. Differences in the measured skills, outcomes, and samples prevent a direct comparison of magnitudes.

The school component also changes how the equalization result should be interpreted. In Korea, recipients gain `r fmt(cfest('KOR','recipient_change'))` predicted reading points, while the gap narrows by `r fmt(cfest('KOR','gap_reduction'))` points because advantaged classmates also gain. @jackson2020school show that schools' contributions to socio-emotional development predict later attainment beyond their contributions to test scores. Their findings establish schools as settings in which these capabilities can develop. The present counterfactual extends the distributional question to classmates: gains for disadvantaged pupils reduce the achievement gap only to the extent that they exceed gains among the advantaged comparison group.

Germany illustrates substantial school-level inequality outside the measured skills pathway. In Korea, predicted recipient gains exceed gap reduction. Denmark combines a positive skills pathway with little amplification from sorting. These contrasting cases show why the skills pathway and the distribution of its predicted benefits both matter. Identifying the institutions behind those differences requires further evidence. The cross-system averages give equal weight to participating systems' assessed complete-case samples and do not represent the global pupil population.

```{=latex}
\begin{revision}
```

For educational policy, socio-economic inequality in socio-emotional skills directs attention to unequal opportunities to develop and use these skills. Instruction, enrichment, and support may contribute jointly to learning and socio-emotional development, as evidence on teachers' and schools' broader contributions suggests [@jackson2018; @jackson2020school]. The possibility that these inputs reinforce each other provides an economic rationale for evaluating them jointly. The equalization benchmark shows how observed skill differences relate to the reading gap under the fitted model. Policy comparisons require evidence on achievable changes, causal learning responses, benefits to classmates, and costs. Substantial inequality outside the measured skills pathway also argues for examining teaching and school resources alongside skill-focused support.

```{=latex}
\end{revision}
```

## Research limitations

The main identification problem is the timing of skills and learning. PISA measures both at the same assessment and provides no prior achievement measure for this analysis. Curiosity may support learning and also respond to it. Unobserved family investments and selection into schools can influence both outcomes. The mediation estimates therefore describe model-based pathways, without identifying causal effects. A causal interpretation would require temporal ordering, sufficient control of confounding, overlap, and correctly specified models.

The equalization exercise adds an assumption about transferability: disadvantaged pupils would have the same fitted reading response to the donor skill profiles in their existing schools. Observed profiles provide an empirical benchmark, but do not establish conditional overlap or show what a feasible intervention could achieve. The additive specification also leaves the ordering and complementarities among skills unestimated. School-average skills combine measurement error with differences in pupils and educational environments, so their coefficients cannot isolate peer effects [@ludtke2008].

Measurement and sample coverage further limit comparisons across systems. The skills are self-reported, and complete-case selection is especially pronounced in Armenia and Lebanon. Country estimates and their equal-weight averages describe the retained analytic samples.


# Conclusion

```{=latex}
\begin{revision}
```

The findings establish a socio-economic gradient in socio-emotional skills, whose relationships with reading account statistically for part of socio-economic learning inequality across the participating systems. Curiosity contributes most widely, while the composition of the pathway varies across countries. These findings are consistent with skills participating in the reproduction of advantage, without establishing whether skills precede learning, respond to it, or develop reciprocally with it.

```{=latex}
\end{revision}
```

The decomposition locates the total gradient and its skills-mediated component within and between schools. Germany illustrates how substantial between-school inequality can coexist with a small measured skills component. Sorting measures the additional pathway associated with the school composition accompanying family rank. Equalization projects changes in achievement after replacing disadvantaged pupils' skill profiles while holding school membership fixed. Predicted gains among advantaged classmates make gap reduction smaller than recipient gains in Korea.

Skills development therefore warrants evaluation alongside improvements in teaching and school resources. Such evaluations need evidence on achievable changes, causal learning responses, who benefits, and costs. Their distributional assessment must distinguish gains for disadvantaged pupils from reductions in the achievement gap.
